lines.text: Meera's support bot for a Bengaluru food app keeps getting things wrong. Her first instinct: fine-tune it.
But a model fails for three different reasons, and each one has a different fix.
Failure one: the reply is an essay when she wanted two lines. The model wasn't told. So fix the prompt.
Add the rule, add an example, run it again. That takes seconds, not days.
Failure two: it quotes last year's refund policy. The model doesn't know. That's missing knowledge, so retrieve the right document. That's RAG.
Update the document, and the answer updates. No training.
Failure three: the facts are right, but one reply in five sounds stiff, not like the brand's Hinglish, even with examples in the prompt.
That's behaviour. Now fine-tuning makes sense: train on a few hundred approved replies.
So climb in order: prompt, then RAG, then fine-tune. Cheapest first, and measure before every step.
And never fine-tune facts that change. Changing knowledge belongs in retrieval, not in weights.
The line to remember: prompting changes instructions, RAG changes knowledge, fine-tuning changes behaviour.
Next lesson: LoRA fine-tuning on a free Colab GPU.
